Montesquieu and climate theory
[edit]French geopolitical doctrines broadly opposed to German Geopolitik and reject the idea of a fixed geography. French geography is focused on the evolution of polymorphic territories being the result of mankind's actions. It also relies on the consideration of long time periods through a refusal to take specific events into account. This method has been theorized by Professor Lacoste according to three principles: Representation; Diachronie; and Diatopie.
In The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu outlined the view that man and societies are influenced by climate. He believed that hotter climates create hot-tempered people and colder climates aloof people, whereas the mild climate of France is ideal for political systems. Considered one of the founders of French geopolitics, Élisée Reclus, is the author of a book considered a reference in modern geography (Nouvelle Géographie universelle). Alike Ratzel, he considers geography through a global vision. However, in complete opposition to Ratzel's vision, Reclus considers geography not to be unchanging; it is supposed to evolve commensurately to the development of human society. His marginal political views resulted in his rejection by academia.
Ancel, Braudel, and the rejection of determinism
[edit]French geographer and geopolitician Jacques Ancel (1879–1936) is considered to be the first theoretician of geopolitics in France, and gave a notable series of lectures at the European Center of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Paris and published Géopolitique in 1936. Like Reclus, Ancel rejects German determinist views on geopolitics (including Haushofer's doctrines).
Braudel's broad view used insights from other social sciences, employed the concept of the longue durée, and downplayed the importance of specific events. This method was inspired by the French geographer Paul Vidal de la Blache (who in turn was influenced by German thought, particularly that of Friedrich Ratzel whom he had met in Germany). Braudel's method was to analyse the interdependence between individuals and their environment.[41] Vidalian geopolitics is based on varied forms of cartography and on possibilism (founded on a societal approach of geography—i.e. on the principle of spaces polymorphic faces depending from many factors among them mankind, culture, and ideas) as opposed to determinism.
Lacoste and the renaissance of French geopolitics
[edit]Due to the influence of German Geopolitik on French geopolitics, the latter were for a long time banished from academic works. In the mid-1970s, Yves Lacoste—a French geographer who was directly inspired by Ancel, Braudel and Vidal de la Blache—wrote La géographie, ça sert d'abord à faire la guerre (Geography first use is war) in 1976. This book symbolizes the birth of this new school of geopolitics (if not so far the first French school of geopolitics as Ancel was very isolated in the 1930s–40s). Initially linked with communist party evolved to a less liberal approach. At the end of the 1980s he founded the Institut Français de Géopolitique (French Institute for Geopolitics) that publishes the Hérodote revue. While rejecting the generalizations and broad abstractions employed by the German and Anglo-American traditions (and the new geographers), this school does focus on spatial dimension of geopolitics affairs on different levels of analysis. This approach emphasizes the importance of multi-level (or multi-scales) analysis and maps at the opposite of critical geopolitics which avoid such tools. Lacoste proposed that every conflict (both local or global) can be considered from a perspective grounded in three assumptions:
- Representation: Each group or individuals is the product of an education and is characterized by specific representations of the world or others groups or individuals. Thus, basic societal beliefs are grounded in their ethnicity or specific location. The study of representation is a common point with the more contemporary critical geopolitics. Both are connected with the work of Henri Lefebvre (La production de l'espace, first published in 1974)
- Diachronie. Conducting an historical analysis confronting "long periods" and short periods as the prominent French historian Fernand Braudel suggested.
- Diatopie: Conducting a cartographic survey through a multi-scale mapping.
Connected with this stream, and former member of Hérodote editorial board, the French geographer Michel Foucher developed a long term analysis of international borders. He coined various neologism among them: Horogenesis: Neologism that describes the concept of studying the birth of borders, Dyade: border shared by two neighbouring states (for instance US territory has two terrestrial dyades : one with Canada and one with Mexico). The main book of this searcher "Fronts et frontières" (Fronts and borders) first published in 1991, without equivalent remains untranslated in English. Michel Foucher is an expert of the African Union for borders affairs.
More or less connected with this school, Stéphane Rosière can be quoted as the editor in Chief of the online journal L'Espace politique, this journal created in 2007 became the most prominent French journal of political geography and Geopolitics with Hérodote.[42]
French philosopher Michel Foucault's dispositif introduced for the purpose of biopolitical research was also adopted in the field of geopolitical thought where it now plays a role.[43]
Russia
[edit]The geopolitical stance adopted by Russia has traditionally been informed by a Eurasian perspective, and Russia's location provides a degree of continuity between the Tsarist and Soviet geostrategic stance and the position of Russia in the international order.[44] In the 1990s, a senior researcher at the Institute of Philosophy, Russian Academy of Sciences of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Vadim Tsymbursky (1957–2009), coined the term "island-Russia" and developed the "Great Limitrophe" concept.
Colonel-General Leonid Ivashov (retired), a Russian geopolitics specialist of the early 21st century, headed the Academy of Geopolitical Problems (Russian: Академия геополитических проблем), which analyzes the international and domestic situations and develops geopolitical doctrine. Earlier, he headed the Main Directorate for International Military Cooperation of the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation.
Vladimir Karyakin, leading researcher at the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, has proposed the term "geopolitics of the third wave".[45][clarification needed]
Aleksandr Dugin, a Russian political analyst who has developed a close relationship with Russia's Academy of the General Staff wrote "The Foundations of Geopolitics: The Geopolitical Future of Russia" in 1997, which has had a large influence within the Russian military, police, and foreign policy elites [46] and it has been used as a textbook in the Academy of the General Staff of the Russian military.[47][46] Its publication in 1997 was well received in Russia and powerful Russian political figures subsequently took an interest in Dugin.[48]
China
[edit]In the early 21st century, according to the report of the National Bureau of Asian Research, the main concern of the Chinese geopolitical experts was what they regarded as the US geopolitical challenge. They viewed the US geopolitics in line with the doctrines of Spykman and Brzezinski, namely the containment of Eurasian peer competitors to perpetuate the US hegemony. Yesterday’s Containment of the Soviet Union and today’s Indo-Pacific strategy are identical in both aim and means. These means include the US-led network of military alliances providing the US with strategic bridgeheads and expansion of what the US 2001 Quadrennial Defense Review called the “geostrategic encirclement of China’s maritime environment". The major difference with the Cold War era is that the Pentagon identified the rise of China as its biggest future challenge, surpassing the threat posed by the Soviet Union The US treats what Spykman called the Eurasian Rimland as geopolitical battleground. One conviction shared by the Chinese, Russian and Anglo-American geopolitical schools, is that Eurasia is the main springboard to world hegemony and will remain the focal region of great-power competition.[49]
According to Li Lingqun, a major feature of the People's Republic of China's geopolitics is attempting to change the laws of the sea to advance claims in the South China Sea.[50] Another geopolitical issue is PRC's claims over the territories of Taiwan against the government of the Republic of China.[51]
Various analysts state that China created the Belt and Road Initiative as a geostrategic effort to take a larger role in global affairs, and undermine what the Communist Party perceives as American hegemony.[52][53][54] It has also been argued that China co-founded the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and New Development Bank to compete with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in development finance.[55][56] According to Bobo Lo, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization has been advertised as a "political organization of a new type" claimed to transcend geopolitics.[57] Political scientist Pak Nung Wong says that a major form of geopolitics between the US and China includes cybersecurity competition, policy regulations regarding technology standards and social media platforms, and traditional and non-traditional forms of espionage.[58]
One view of the New Great Game is a shift to geoeconomic compared to geopolitical competition. The interest in oil and gas includes pipelines that transmit energy to China's east coast. Xiangming Chen believes that China's role is more like Britain's than Russia's in the New Great Game, where Russia plays the role that the Russian Empire originally did. Chen stated, "Regardless of the prospect, China through the BRI is deep in playing a 'New Great Game' in Central Asia that differs considerably from its historical precedent about 150 years ago when Britain and Russia jostled with each other on the Eurasian steppes."[59] In the Carnegie Endowment, Paul Stronski and Nicole Ng wrote in 2018 that China has not fundamentally challenged any Russian interests in Central Asia.[60]
Geopolitical attention has expanded to encompass the supply chains of critical materials, alongside competition over their production, processing, and the manufacture of clean energy technologies.[61][62] China became a major producer of solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles, and a leading processor of many critical minerals.[63]

articles.title: Continuing resolution could ‘complicate’ Army’s HADES spy plane production: Official
articles.snippet: The Army’s G-2 Andrew Evans told Breaking Defense the program is currently “completely” on cost and schedule, but a budget impasse threatens plans.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Army’s new spy plane program remains on track, but if lawmakers delay passing a 2027 budget, the service will not be able to move into production as planned, a senior defense official warned.
“We actually are still completely on cost with the program and completely on schedule, which is somewhat rare across the department,” Andrew Evans, the director for the Strategy & Transformation Office inside the Army’s Deputy Chief of Staff for Intelligence shop (G-2), told Breaking Defense.
“However, the CR [continuing resolution], which is out of our hands, does complicate that. So next year at this time, will I be able to say the same thing? I don’t know,” he added on the sidelines of the Annual Association of the US Army conference.
RELATED: Can’t start, won’t start: Over 150 new military programs face delay under CR
So far, the Army is moving out with development of three High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System (HADES) prototypes — Bombardier Global 6500 jets that Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) is outfitting with different tech packages. The first prototype, according to Evans, is slated to be delivered around the January 2027 timeframe and will be used in an operational demonstration to ensure that “everything from aperture to analytics is all connecting.” After that it will be made available to Pentagon leaders to decide how to use the collection asset.
“They will tell us what their priority is, and the asset will fly to that area and begin collection operations,” Evans said.
The second prototype should be delivered roughly six months later, and the third one, which is “significantly advanced from the first two,” is slated for delivery in 2028.
But after those three prototypes, the Army had been eyeing HADES production aircraft and planned to ink a deal with SNC around the start of 2027. However, lawmakers have not approved a fiscal 2027 defense spending bill and are funding the government on a continuing resolution through early December. A spending bill could take even longer given the upcoming midterm elections and Pentagon plans to work with lawmakers to reconfigure the spending request.
If those talks and budget slip further into 2027 or the defense leaders want to pull HADES funding for other priorities, then a production contract could be put on ice.
“We are ready to move in on the ‘27 [plan to] award a production contract for HADES; We cannot do that … until we clear a CR,” Evans said.

articles.title: Polish defense minister calls for US industry to establish European facilities
articles.snippet: Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz spoke the same day that another senior Polish commander said Patriot deliveries to Poland are expected to be delayed.
articles.full_text:
WARSAW — Poland’s national defense minister is calling on Europe to develop an “enduring, predictable” alliance with the US, encompassing information exchange, military capabilities and defense industry collaboration.
“I believe that within the ‘NATO 3.0’ strategy, it is worth emphasizing a strategy for the defense industry,” Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told the Warsaw Security Conference on Monday. “Relocating production lines and maintenance facilities to Europe, for instance, for Patriot missiles and systems, is crucial for the independence of both the United States and Europe.”
The comments arrived on the same day that Polish army operational commander Gen. Ireneusz Nowak noted at the event that Patriot deliveries are set to be held up. “At this point it looks like we are going to be affected as well,” he said. “That’s very visible in the area of PAC-3 MSE Patriot missiles, they’re going to be delayed for sure.”
Ukraine has called on European partners to supply it with additional Patriot missiles to fend off Russian attacks. Kosiniak-Kamysz said the current situation in Ukraine shows how dangerous a breakdown in supply chains would be in a crisis scenario, so Europe must do everything to be strong and independent enough to take action toward greater reindustrialization.
Additionally, he warned that the European Union has been grappling with the issue of military mobility for years, and “yet, there are still no decisions in place to allow for the free movement of our troops without requiring the consent of individual regions.”
The matter needs to be resolved as soon as possible, he stressed, through the adoption of sound legislation. “It should be automatic: if someone calls for help, they want those troops to reach them, and everyone else should provide support,” he explained.
From a big picture perspective, Europe cannot wait until 2035 to become strong, said Kosiniak-Kamysz, as he argued that NATO’s 5 percent GDP defense spending pledge should be brought forward to 2030.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said Europe must make its defense industry supply chains independent, and this is a task that needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency, because “we cannot rule out equipment from outside the European Union if it is critically needed.”
In his view, it stands to reason that collaboration with the US on items like low-cost, long-range precision strike capabilities, drones and anti-drone systems, as well as artificial intelligence, could prove worthwhile.
“So let us not rule out the possibility of creating Polish-US or European-US joint ventures, that could also tap into [SAFE] European funds,” he said. Of the €44 billion ($49 billion) from the SAFE program, nearly one-third went to Poland, and two-thirds of that amount has already been allocated to the Polish defense industry.
At a strategic level, he also declared that Poland is stronger with Washington’s backing.
“The more American troops there are in Poland, and if we have a permanent base and a lasting American military presence, the better equipped we are to shoulder responsibility for NATO’s eastern flank,” he said.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said also Warsaw will be ready for full-scale deterrence, thanks to investments in the defense industry, military mobility, transatlantic cooperation, relocating production to Europe, and joint investments in critical defense capabilities.
Speaking alongside Kosiniak-Kamysz, Minister of National Defence of Lithuania Robertas Kaunas said in the case of a Russian attack against Lithuania, it might be two weeks before US, Polish, German, British troops could arrive and reach the Soviet border to Lithuania. He echoed Kosiniak-Kamysz words, saying his country is investing in a national division, and an anti-drone air defense system, combining all different types of sensors, under a single ecosystem, backed by artificial intelligence.
Elsewhere, NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska said that different things required to implement the alliance’s newly unveiled “theory of victory,” includes logistics, procurement and intelligence. “NATO is able to defend us. … But in order for all of us to keep this strategic advantage that we have [to] invest, create the capabilities, apply them, employ them, train the troops,” she said.
Shekerinska said NATO needs to speed up procurement procedures “to prepare [a] completely new approach in what is the capability, and how to make sure that NATO will have them when it will be needed.”
Rounding off panelist contributions, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, Poland’s Secretary of State for Defense, said she hopes the moment has come for the US government and US companies to finally agree on co-production in Europe, as US warehouses are empty. According to her, Warsaw is open to other countries, setting up shop in Poland for maintenance, logistics or production.
“If there’s any foreign company trying to sell something to us, we are not only looking on the quality and price, we give four extra conditions: the maintenance center, co-production, local suppliers or at least investing in education here,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka stressed. She added that the issue of standing up local maintenance centers is one the Polish government is trying to resolve with from Washington.
“We are open for co-production, we are open … [to] companies from different parts of the world, but the condition is you have to work with our industry,” she concluded.

articles.title: Army to take a (cautious) step toward employing AI agents to defend networks: Official
articles.snippet: The Army is making its first awards under Project Griffin, which eventually envisions AI prowling networks for malicious activity.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army is poised to take its next step toward potentially unleashing defensive AI agents on its networks as the service plans to award contracts to two companies by the end of the week, a key official said.
“The one that we plan to award on Friday is our take action element. So essentially, how are we not only autonomously detecting a potential adversary? How are we now doing something — having an autonomous response within prescribed parameters of a human operator, or even in conjunction with that?” Brandon Pugh, the service’s principal cyber advisor, said at the annual AUSA conference on Monday. “That is extraordinary. Something we haven’t done and we’re very excited about.”
Pugh declined to provide the names of the awardees ahead of the Friday announcement.
The network AI effort, dubbed Project Griffin, stemmed from a tabletop exercise with top industry executives and service leaders. The Army published a commercial solutions opening in August, spurring 108 submissions that were narrowed to 10 finalists.
Pugh explained that the Army has tools, such as its Panoptic Junction capability, that he said have a nearly 90 percent success rate at identifying malicious activity on the network. But they don’t currently have a way at remediating or remedying those threats, especially with limited humans.
Despite the award on Friday, officials said agents won’t begin work on government networks immediately.
“For us, it’s going to be: Are we as humans ready to let the agent actually take action? You think about that for how many years a human has been the person making the patch, remediating something, so we’re walking ourselves through what does it mean to have an agent to do that work and then how do you check that agent’s work. So a lot still to do in this space,” Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank, commander of Army Cyber Command, told reporters at the conference.
He added that the service is working with companies to understand where what they can do in this space and determine what does it actually mean to take action, noting they’re working “hand-in-hand with the companies to build out what it looks like” and then put it through a deliberate process on the Army’s portion of the network. The two companies awarded could work in tandem on the effort or do their own thing.
Pugh said that using a commercial solutions opening to gather ideas was actually suggested by members of industry, as a way to keep responses broad as opposed to prescribing what companies should provide to the Army. Industry oftentimes has capabilities or ideas that aren’t even on the government’s radar, he said.
Given the big aperture, the Army wants to figure out what the companies are capable of providing as they put it through its paces.

articles.title: Sandbox vulnerability gives rogue AI agents a path to escape and leak data, research says
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The new research, published by AI security startup AIR, found that a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox — a tool used to run code in isolated environments — could allow agents to exploit certificate validation processes to transmit data outside approved networks.
articles.full_text:
Sandbox vulnerability gives rogue AI agents a path to escape and leak data, research says
Cybersecurity researchers on Monday said they discovered a vulnerability in a widely used AI development sandbox that could allow rogue agents to leak sensitive information by bypassing restrictions designed to keep them isolated.
The new research, published by AI security startup AIR, found that a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox — a tool used to run code in isolated environments — could allow agents to exploit certificate validation processes to transmit data outside approved networks.
“This vulnerability shows that enterprises can have Hugging Face [style] mini incidents with their own agents,” Niv Hoffman, AIR co-founder and CTO, told Recorded Future News in an interview.
“The new contribution our research makes is [showing] that even in the standard hardened sandbox of today, there are still flaws that will make an agent going rogue manage to escape the sandbox and do things in the wild.”
Developers typically use sandboxes to prevent AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems or transmitting sensitive information. Network allowlists restrict communication to approved destinations, preventing agents from connecting to untrusted servers.
AIR researchers found that rogue agents could circumvent those restrictions by exploiting the way servers handle digital certificates. In a scenario demonstrated by the researchers, a specific certificate was designed that could be sent to an approved server and could then trigger a request to an attacker-controlled server, allowing the information to be transmitted without the sandbox ever directly communicating with the unauthorized destination.
“A crafted certificate is all it takes,” the report said. “The wall meant to keep your secrets in has a door, and the agent holds the key.”
“It’s a very hard leak to patch,” Hoffman said. “This sandbox never communicated directly with the attack server… so from the sandbox perspective, everything looked fine.”
Hoffman said his team contacted Vercel about the vulnerability and the company said it needs time to find a patch because “it's unclear for them right now how it's going to be done.”
Vercel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
AIR has not found evidence of any exploitation of the vulnerability in the wild, but can’t rule out whether or not there has been one, Hoffman said, underscoring that the vulnerability in the Vercel sandbox appeared to be longstanding.
The research is important because it shows that an approved server can become an “unwitting courier for stolen credentials,” according to Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, a cyberkinetics company. “Security has to account for what happens after the first connection.”
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: West African scam compounds raided, more than 100 suspected trafficking victims ‘rescued’
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: More than two dozen people were arrested by police in Ghana and Nigeria as part of a U.K.-hosted operation that also included tech companies.
articles.full_text:
West African scam compounds raided, more than 100 suspected trafficking victims ‘rescued’
Police in Ghana and Nigeria arrested or detained 28 people and identified more than 100 suspected victims of human trafficking during an international operation targeting scam compounds in West Africa, U.S. and British officials announced Tuesday.
The operation was hosted by Britain’s National Crime Agency (NCA) in London last week. It brought together 15 law enforcement agencies and the same number of tech companies — including Meta, Microsoft and Google — as part of what they called Joint Disruption Week.
In Ghana, authorities raided a compound in Sasaabi, a semi-rural community outside the capital, Accra, arresting 19 people and seizing 303 devices, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Nigerian authorities made nine further arrests.
The Ghanaian police also identified 117 people whom the department described as trafficking victims and said were “rescued” and now awaiting repatriation to Nigeria, alongside 89 scam victims who had lost an estimated $8.3 million.
“These networks steal savings on one side of the screen, and people’s freedom on the other,” said Matthew Floyd, a deputy assistant director in the FBI’s Criminal Division.
The Department of Justice said the technology companies it worked with removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages and groups linked to the West African scam centres.
Meta’s Rob Cochrane gave the same figure for Facebook and Instagram alone. The department did not break the total down by company.
“The disrupted schemes included law enforcement impersonation scams, digital ‘arrest’ extortion schemes, cryptocurrency investment fraud (also known as ‘pig butchering’), and a variety of other online fraud operations targeting global victims,” stated the DOJ.
Following the police action in West Africa, officials said more than $11 million in “potentially freezable” funds had been identified, but did not say how much had been frozen or seized. The FBI’s Floyd described identifying assets as “the easy part.”
Nick Sharp, the NCA’s deputy director of fraud, said it was not yet known how many British or American victims the compounds had targeted, as forensic work on seized devices continues.
The Meta connection
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said the operation began with information from Meta, which the NCA also credited as playing “a key role in coordinating the event and encouraging broad private sector participation to maximize scam compound disruption.”
Pirro — a former Fox News host and longtime ally of President Donald Trump — said she was “very proud to work with Meta.” She credited all of the participating businesses with having “voluntarily disrupted scam infrastructure” on their platforms, adding: “And thank God for them.”
Her praise for Meta comes as the company faces scrutiny over fraud on its platforms and questions about whether the right incentives exist for the company to properly tackle such fraud.
A Reuters investigation last year, citing internal company documents, reported that Meta projected about 10% of its 2024 revenue, roughly $16 billion, would come from ads linked to scams and banned goods. Meta disputes that figure and says scams undermine the trust its advertising business depends on.
Last November, Sens. Richard Blumenthal, (D-CT) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) urged the Federal Trade Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether Meta profited from scam advertising and whether enforcement action was warranted.
Other lawmakers have pushed for broader changes. In February, Sens. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and Bernie Moreno (R-OH) introduced the bipartisan SCAM Act, which would require social media companies to take “reasonable steps” to verify advertisers and combat fraudulent ads or face action from the FTC and state attorneys general.
Earlier this year, Trump signed an executive order focused on cybercrime, fraud and scam centers, emphasizing law enforcement coordination, diplomacy and victim restitution rather than imposing direct new obligations on tech platforms.
Asked by Recorded Future News whether Meta would require identity verification for all advertisers, Cochrane pointed to earlier targets for verifying high-risk advertisers.
The company said it is aiming for verified advertisers to account for 90% of its ad revenue by the end of 2026, up from 70% today, arguing that the remaining 10% would low-risk unverified businesses such as “local ice cream shops.”

articles.title: North Korean hackers target Ukrainian experts for possible intelligence on Russia's war
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: North Korean hackers have been targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy amid Pyongyang’s growing military cooperation with Russia.
articles.full_text:
North Korean hackers target Ukrainian experts for possible intelligence on Russia's war
North Korean hackers have been targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy amid Pyongyang’s growing military cooperation with Russia, according to a new report.
As part of the campaign, the hacking group Kimsuky used fake conference invitations, research collaboration requests and malicious documents designed to steal information, South Korean cybersecurity firm Genians said in a report published Monday.
North Korea has provided troops to fight in the war in Ukraine as well as other military support to Russia since 2024.
"Kimsuky’s attacks against Ukraine may be aimed at collecting information on the war, the extent of North Korean troop losses, developments in the questioning and handling of prisoners of war, and the details of consultations between South Korea and Ukraine,” researchers said, adding that most of the observed attacks were unsuccessful.
Genians said the transfer of two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces to South Korea in September could also be of intelligence interest to Pyongyang, particularly what the prisoners might disclose about North Korean military operations and casualties.
Operation GitPower
In one attack in August, the hackers impersonated organizers of a cybersecurity conference in Seoul and invited a Ukrainian security expert to speak at the event.
The email included genuine details about the conference and offered to cover travel and accommodation expenses. It initially did not contain malicious links or attachments. Instead, the attackers encouraged the recipient to respond before sending additional materials.
In another case, the hackers posed as a European policy researcher seeking feedback on a report about military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. After the recipient responded, the attackers sent a link to a malicious archive disguised as research material, according to Genians.
The hackers also used files disguised as PDF documents and legitimate Zoom installers to trick recipients into running malicious software. The malware was designed to collect information from infected computers, maintain access to compromised systems and send stolen information to infrastructure controlled by the attackers.
Researchers also identified Japanese-language documents on infrastructure associated with the campaign, suggesting the hackers may have been preparing attacks against Japanese-speaking targets.
These attacks are part of a broader cyberespionage campaign tracked as Operation GitPower, which uses legitimate software development platforms, including GitHub, GitLab and Codeberg, to distribute malicious files and communicate with compromised systems, researchers said.
Broader espionage campaign
Kimsuky has been active since at least 2012, targeting governments, think tanks, academics, and media organizations across Asia, Europe, Japan, Russia and the United States. In 2023, the U.S. and its Pacific allies imposed sanctions on the group, accusing it of collecting intelligence to support North Korea’s foreign policy and sanctions-evasion efforts.
In May 2025, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reported that a North Korean-linked group tracked as TA406 had been sending malicious emails to Ukrainian government agencies, potentially seeking intelligence about the risks facing North Korean troops fighting alongside Russian forces.
According to Proofpoint, TA406’s cyber operations in Ukraine focus on political intelligence and strategic analysis of the war, in contrast to Russian hackers, who typically seek tactical intelligence related to battlefield operations.

is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Russian internet provider SkyNet reports outages after cyberattack claimed by Ukrainian hackers
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: One of St. Petersburg's major internet providers said its network had been under a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack since October 6, affecting services including online gaming, voice calls and video conferencing.
articles.full_text:
Russian internet provider SkyNet reports outages after cyberattack claimed by Ukrainian hackers
A major internet provider in Russia's second-largest city, St. Petersburg, has reported days of service disruptions following a cyberattack claimed by a Ukrainian hacking group.
SkyNet said in a statement on Friday that its network had been disrupted by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack since October 6, affecting services including online gaming, voice calls and video conferencing.
The company said customers could experience slow connections, high latency and interruptions to audio and video services as it worked to mitigate the attack. It did not say when normal operations would resume.
SkyNet customers were still reporting connectivity problems on Tuesday, according to Russian internet outage monitoring service Detector404. Complaints included fiber-optic internet outages, Wi-Fi connectivity failures and high connection latency.
The Ukrainian hacking group BO Team claimed responsibility for attacks on SkyNet's infrastructure on September 14 and October 5, saying it had disabled more than 15,000 network devices.
"A quick recovery will not be possible," the group added in a statement over the weekend.
The group also published screenshots purportedly showing access to SkyNet's internal systems. The company has not confirmed the hackers' claims about disabled equipment or unauthorized access to its systems.
BO Team described the operation as retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers, referring to Moscow's use of the term "digital detox" in connection with the attacks.
SkyNet, which has operated since 2003, provides residential and business internet access, digital television, telephone services and data center services in St. Petersburg.
The company previously experienced a major outage in mid-September, which it attributed to a technical failure. Some customers reported connectivity problems for several days. It remains unclear whether that incident was connected to BO Team's claimed September 14 attack.
BO Team, also known as Black Owl, emerged in early 2024 and has since claimed attacks on several Russian telecommunications providers, including Vega-Internet, Kraft-S, SimStar and Orion Telecom.
The group has previously collaborated with Ukrainian military intelligence on operations targeting Russian organizations, including a drone supplier, a federal digital signature authority and a scientific research center.
Russian cybersecurity company Kaspersky said in a report that BO Team had expanded its operations beyond disruptive attacks to include cyber espionage and more covert intrusions. According to Kaspersky, the group targeted 20 organizations in the first quarter of 2026, increasingly focusing on manufacturing, telecommunications and oil and gas companies.
Researchers said the group typically gained initial access through targeted phishing emails carrying malicious attachments and used backdoors and other malware to maintain access to compromised networks.
Kaspersky described BO Team as operating more independently than many other pro-Ukrainian hacking groups, with its own resources and methods.
"BO Team remains a serious and continuously evolving threat in the Russian cyber threat landscape," the researchers said.

articles.title: Ledger says hardware implant in cryptocurrency wallets stole recovery phrases
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ledger cryptocurrency wallets sold through a Southeast Asian reseller had an implant allowing outsiders to drain funds, the company said.
articles.full_text:
Ledger says hardware implant in cryptocurrency wallets stole recovery phrases
Cryptocurrency wallet maker Ledger said Tuesday that devices sold through Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis contained hidden hardware implants that captured users’ recovery phrases, allowing attackers to steal their funds.
In a series of social media posts, the Paris-based company said its security research team found the affected devices contained implants that read data displayed on the screens.
During setup, the implants detect users’ 24-word recovery phrase and transmit it over an LTE connection using an embedded eSIM. Unknown attackers subsequently used the phrase to access users’ funds.
Those funds were drained last week, on Oct. 9. Ledger said it has not confirmed the total losses and urged caution against speculation.
“If you bought a Ledger signer from CryptoBilis and have not set it up, do not set it up and contact Ledger Support. If you have set it up, transfer your assets promptly to a new signer with a new recovery phrase,” the company said.
“Do not enter or restore any recovery phrase on a signer bought from CryptoBilis,” its statement added.
Ledger said all confirmed thefts, which have largely been reported within Southeast Asia, involve devices sold through CryptoBilis — but it added it is “also reviewing reports of implants in other signers and locations.”
In a notice on its website, CryptoBilis linked to the Ledger warning and said it has “paused all sales and shipments of Ledger devices while Ledger investigates,” and said it was “cooperating fully with Ledger’s investigation.”
Ledger has not identified the affected models, but warned that because the implants leave one of its key security features, the Secure Element, intact, tampered devices may still pass the company’s authenticity checks.
Ledger urged CryptoBilis customers not to activate unused devices and advised those already using them to promptly transfer funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase.
The company said victims should reach out to them and to local law enforcement before opening or shipping affected devices. It added that it believes the “volume of impacted devices is limited.”

articles.title: FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm
articles.snippet: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested the co-founder of a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
articles.full_text:
Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.
The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.
One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.
An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.
According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.
[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in November 2025].
“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.
Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”
The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.
Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”
“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”
Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.
ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.
Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.
Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.
This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.
The irony here is hard to miss. The industry sells “communicating with a criminal isn’t the same as paying” as a clean distinction, but the line between negotiator and middleman gets blurry fast when the same people sit between victims and extortionists. Charges are only allegations at this point, but if the other firms Brian mentions get charged too, expect a lot more scrutiny of how ransomware negotiators operate and who they’re really accountable to.
It’s worse than ironic, it’s sadly common these days in most fields. Once the commercial motive is introduced, there’s a *huge* incentive for the people involved to perpetuate the problem rather than solve it. I think I first ran into it in the early days of the anti-spam efforts, where working solutions were sidelined in favor of poorly functioning technologies that mostly served to give monopoly players control of deliverability. The email phishing that leads to ransomware gangs like Shiny Hunters simply *would not happen* if people just wised up to the fact that these trillion dollar companies aren’t giving you technology advice that works in *your* best interest.
So the FBI got another low-level “dealer”. Great. Now let’s see how long it takes them to round up *anyone* from the Epstein-class “supplier” organizations.
I love your articles. Great work.
The very least the FBI could do would be to post these filth hackass addresses, bank information, family records, social securities, phone numbers and what not, so they end up eaten alive by the same annoyance they created.
Die by the sword bastards.
Somehow I doubt this government is providing any finders-fees for your work, keep up the good work Krebs.
Also I can’t find the direct contact for you anymore, but the comment interface is pretty wonky on my phone, in that the submit button has some odd coloring on my phone, making it hard to see in light mode and almost impossible to see in dark mode. Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.
That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.
The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.
We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.
https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others
The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.
Well, Van der Stap also worked in the industry, doing offensive security while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerable Disclosure, and it’s well-established that ShinyHunters actively sought to recruit insiders employed at key targets, particularly telecom providers (…while making it very clear they don’t target companies in Russia, Belarus, North Korea, and China… but sure, they are “purely financially motivated”).
Fully expecting that as the FBI and European authorities dig deeper, quite a few more people will be found actively playing both sides of the fence.
The line between ‘mediating’ an extortion attempt and actively facilitating a federal crime has always been razor-thin in this industry. If negotiators are taking a cut of the payout or coordinating directly with groups like ShinyHunters beyond strict incident response, it’s no longer advisory—it’s collusion. Expect cyber insurance carriers to drastically overhaul their IR vendor requirements after this.
If we can’t trust our colleagues on the good side; where do, we go from here with insider threats? With privacy and data protection laws, how can we ferret out operatives that are dual-role actors? In espionage, the double agent? Integrity and trust become obsolete.
There is an additional important question about the whole FBI leak affair that needs to be answered: Who in the FBI moved these sensitive personnel files to a server that could be penetrated by outsiders? My guess is that somebody in DOGE did it, in preparation for downloading the files to the DOGE network outside the FBI. This might also mean that private parties in the U.S. have had these files for a long time.
Perhaps the next administration will want to get to the bottom of this and punish the perpetrators, if any. The Trump administration most certainly will not.
The breached application is Oracle PeopleSoft — specifically, an unpatched vulnerability in its Environment Management Hub platform tracked as CVE-2026-35273. According to reports last week, the FBI removed an Accenture contractor that was responsible for keeping it updated.
Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the
practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is
visibility into what the group actually does to get in.
Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration
chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:
– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect,
Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability.
– Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early.
– Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting
thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one
transfer to be useful to the extortion side.
The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside
the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small
repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.
We covered the detection angle in more depth here:
https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest
The detail about the arrest happening while he was in town for the Cyber Risk Summit at the Loews is wild, feels like it was ripped from a thriller. I get that ransomware response is high stakes, but a negotiation firm being linked to the group it’s supposed to be fighting is a huge trust problem. For stuff like cleaning up product images at scale I just use a bulk background remover and move on, but clearly cybercrime is a whole different mess.

And it’s a now legitimate SaaS.

What a terrible joke.
Not sure why this is being mentioned like something abnormal: “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”.
Any reputable IR firm does exactly that. It is so valuable, that threat actors start denying access to some information. I lost the count of cases where clients felt more relief after we start comms and decided not to pay because of that communication.

articles.title: ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests
articles.snippet: A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle "Rey," was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey's father -- Royal Jordanian Airlines.
articles.full_text:
A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.
On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.
Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.
Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.
As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.
ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.
In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.
Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.
‘REY’ MEANS KING, AS IN ROYAL
According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.
Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.
In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.
“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”
A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”
Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.
However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.
Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.
Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.
MURDER FOR HIRE?
Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.
Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.
Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.
Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.
When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.
“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”
FRANCHISING AND BURNING A BRAND
Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.
More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.
In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.
“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.
A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.
“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”
In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.
The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”
The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”
